In a judgment dated January 4, 1960, following a hearing by the board of
Inquiries of the Ministry transport commissioners relating to the train service being furnished by Canadian Pacific Railway Company on its line between Vancouver, British Columbia, and Medicine Hat, Alberta, via Nelson, B.C., and to inquire into the adequacy thereof and complaints respecting it, the board expressed the opinion that no order should be made at that time upon the railway in respect of its present service between Victoria and Medicine Hat. However, at such time as (a) a sufficient time has elapsed without depredations occurring in the area as to remove, beyond reasonable doubt, the threat to the travelling public and to the railway, or (b) such protective measures have been taken as are, in the opinion of the police forces administering such measures, sufficient to protect the travelling public and the railway, then, if the railway company has not, of its own accord, resumed a service which in the then existing circumstances meets the reasonable needs of the area, an application may be made to this board to require it to do so.

The answer to that question is yes. speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) moved:
subtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I am very pleased that the minister has been able to bring this motion forward this early in the session, and I quite agree-as I did last year-with the desirability of having the committee set up.
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act
However, I have a few suggestions to make with regard to the proceedings of the committee this year which I intend to try to make in a wholly non-controversial way. I recognize that last year most of the members of the committee had had very little experience in this kind of inquiry; that it was exploratory, and that, apart from the hon. gentleman from this house who was the joint chairman, very few of the members of the committee had had any experience of participating in this form of inquiry before.
I do feel that if we are to obtain the maximum advantage from the work of this committee-and I hope we will-a certain amount of assistance will be necessary, and not merely from the Chair. I say this because it does seem to me that this is one of the fields where there is a great need for assistance, a need for direction by the minister and her parliamentary secretary, both of whom will, I hope, be members of the committee. I do not feel that the committee can function effectively unless the minister herself is there as much as possible to give an authoritative opinion on certain points which may arise. It does seem to me that when we are considering a statute as long and as complicated as the Indian Act, unless some lead is given by the superintendent general, some indication as to what sections of the act the government considers may reasonably be regarded as amendable and what sections the government feels need not be amended, in the light of the experience of the administration, the discussion will simply wander all over the lot without any sense of direction, with the result that in the end a lot of meetings will have been held but nothing will have been brought into any kind of focus.
I am sure the minister, after very nearly two years of experience as superintendent general, will agree with the conclusion which I myself reached at the end of three year's of similar work; namely, that it is very hard indeed to make any general rules for application to Indians in all parts of Canada. The law as it applies in some parts of Canada is often unsuitable for application to Indians in other parts of the country-sometimes, indeed, in the same province-having regard to the varying states of economic and social development and also to the differing, and apparently inherent, attitudes of the various bands of Indians.
While we obviously do have today-I regret it, but it is true-a special statute with respect to our Indian population, and I am sure we are going to have one for a long time to come, it is my hope, and I think I am not doing the minister an injustice when I say I believe she expressed it as her hope,

Joint Committee to Study Indian Act that the day will come when there will no longer be any need for an Indian Act or an Indian affairs branch. This is the goal toward which all good administration should work. I do know that there is among the Indians a relatively small but very potent minority that does not take this view at all. The Indians in that minority take the view that they are not Canadian citizens, that they do not want to be Canadian citizens and that they do not want to be treated as Canadian citizens. They take the position that they are a separate nation in alliance with Canada and that they should be treated as such.
That constitutes a serious and special problem particularly in a number of reserves where that view is opposed by another group of Indians who take the view that they are citizens, who want to be considered as citizens and want as rapidly as possible to have all the attributes of citizenship. The minister had to meet that problem in rather regrettable circumstances on one occasion a few months ago, circumstances which I regretted as much, I am sure, as the minister did.
I have no intention at this time of entering into a discussion of that problem. I merely mention it because it is perhaps the most dramatic illustration available of the extreme complexity of the problem and the difficulty of any attempt to provide legislation for people who are largely although not wholly unrepresented in this parliament.
Here again we have the most extraordinary anomalies. Many of the Indians help to elect members to this house because all those who do not live on reserves-whether they do not live on reserves through their own choice or because they have no reserve to live on-have the right to vote for members to this house, as do certain other Indians, including veterans and their wives and those who have signed the waivers, of whom the minister told us today there were only 122; and then there are many Indians, among them the most advanced in the country, who because they choose to go on living on the reserves and do not choose to sign the waiver, do not have any voice in choosing the people who in this house help to make the laws with respect to them.
It is true that there is representation in the other place, if I may make this observation in a completely non-controversial way. There is one honourable gentleman who was appointed, of course on account of his individual merit as was the case with every appointee in that other place, who does happen to be himself an Indian and therefore in a sense, although not in a truly representative sense, the Indians have some representation there.
[Mr. Pickersglll.l
It is therefore, I think, a trust in more senses than perhaps any other piece of legislation we ever have to deal with that we are considering when we consider the Indian Act, first because it deals with the original inhabitants of this country, and because of the relationship which our predecessors had with them of which we cannot always be too proud, and, second, because of the fact that they do not really yet-although I hope that condition is not going to continue for very long-have an adequate voice in determining the laws which apply to them generally or apply to them particularly.
Before any substantial amendments are made to the act, I feel that, in addition to anything that may be done by a parliamentary committee another step should be taken, as was taken by Mr. Harris when he was minister and as I took when I was minister; there should be another meeting arranged with the Indians themselves, and that notwithstanding the fact that it may be, by that time, they will theoretically have the franchise.
A meeting should be arranged with Indians, or representative Indians chosen by the bands themselves, in order to consider the proposals that the government intends to place before parliament for such amendments. I do not say and I am not suggesting that that general proposition should exclude the possibility of certain amendments being made to the Indian Act in the meantime and in particular-if I may just allude to it without attempting to debate it-the measure we are about to consider, when the consideration of the appointment of this committee is concluded.
I know there are many groups in this country, some of them actually the selfchosen representatives of Indian bands and some of them people who have shown a great and devoted interest to the Indians for many years, who wish to make representations to a parliamentary committee and, of course, to that I take no exception whatsoever. However, it is nearly always the case that such representations do not reflect in fact a carefully considered criticism of the whole act. They nearly always deal with some particular grievance of some particular group of Indians or some particular interest of some particular group of Indians and it is not reasonable to expect that by desultory-if I may use that term without	disrespect-representations
made by those who may have come forward to make them, we will get anything like a representative view of what the Indians themselves may want to have done about the legislation.
I assume that, within the limits of what is reasonable and practical, everyone in this

house without distinction of party really wants to do not only what he thinks is good for the Indians but what the Indians themselves want to have done.
It seems to me it is therefore essential that in addition to any representations that may be made by outsiders the committee should have put before it by the minister and her officials with her express approval the suggestions as to those sections of the act which ought to be amended. I do not say categorical views as to how the legislation should be amended because I am sure the minister would not have asked us who are going to be on the committee to give up our time to the work of the committee if she had hard, fast and categorical views that could not be changed by the committee. From such experience as I think most of us have had with matters of this kind I am sure we would all really agree that unless we have put before us a scheme, a set of proposals or an indication of what parts of the act really ought to be taken into account and what parts really need amendment or some guidance of that kind, it is going to be very difficult when the committee's work is completed to have anything to report that will be at once constructive and comprehensive.
It is nearly three years since I had responsibility for the administration of the Indian affairs branch and a great many changes have taken place since that time in the economy and in other respects. I would not presume to say, at this stage, what changes I think ought to be made in the act or in the administration. I do want to say, however, that after three years' experience my own view is that the most important parts of the administration are those which have to do with the education of Indians to which I attach more importance than to anything else, because I am quite convinced that until the aducation of the Indians and the opportunities tor their education are in every way comparable to what is available to other Canadians, no adequate progress will be made. Regrettably this equality does not yet exist although there has been an immense improvement, particularly since Mr. Harris took the administration in hand and the amendments were made in 1952. But, notwithstanding the improvements that have been made, it is certainly not true to say that today on the average the Indians have equal opportunities with other Canadians for education. That, I think, is the most important thing of all if we are to expect Indians ever to become really equal citizens with other Canadians, which I believe every Canadian who is worthy of the name, in his heart, wants to see.
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act
The second thing is that I believe that much more attention needs to be given, much more effort needs to be put into, and much more money needs to be spent upon economic development. This, to my way of thinking, is of the utmost importance. I have never quite recovered from the impression which was made upon my mind by visiting one of the residential schools in Ontario where in fact today-because the educational opportunities are better in Ontario on the average than in most of the provinces, especially in the older parts of Ontario- we find very few children except children of broken homes or orphans and children who, therefore, really, when the school is over have no place to go. I was shocked to realize something that I ought to have known but had never known, I suppose because of lack of imagination. It never occurred to me before that when these children reached the school-leaving age they just went back to the reserve to which they belonged at the school-leaving age of 16. There was no systematic attempt to follow them up to see that they got into constructive lines of employment. I know a good deal has been done since, in the last few years, and I know a great deal of progress has been made in this field; but it is a very important thing to see that after spending all the money that is spent-and it is very expensive to have these Indians go to these residential schools-we should not just abandon them, especially those who have no families, to go back to what all too often turns out to be a road to something rather close to delinquency. It was a gap that certainly existed and that certainly needed to be filled, but I think the most serious of all problems is the problem for which the minister has no responsibility, for which I was not responsible, and unhappily-

I quite agree with you, sir; I am afraid I have tended to abuse the rules of the house a little bit because perhaps of the natural interest I have in the subject.
1898	HOUSE OF
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act Therefore, my remarks may have been irrelevant and perhaps Your Honour is right in jacking me up. I think I can make them quite relevant to the motion by saying I would hope that the committee would concentrate its review, both of the administration and of the legislation, on these particular fields rather than to spread itself over every aspect of the question; first the education field, and second economic development.
The third field I was entering on which, perhaps, raised the point in Your Honour's mind, is the field that I want to say something about and which is directly relating to the motion.
I do hope that the most serious consideration will be given to this most serious problem-I do not say it is the most important problem, but the most difficult problem-of all, and that is the problem of those Indians who leave reserves, who have gone to places that are not really organized into proper municipalities, who live on the periphery of mining camps and other northern settlements and who, because they do not live on reserves, have ceased to be in many respects under the responsibility of the Indian affairs branch. They are really orphans in an administrative and juridical sense. The question of who is responsible for their education and who is responsible for their welfare is one that is very difficult to solve, having regard to the fact that the ministers in the provincial governments are always checked up by their provincial treasurers and the hon. lady, the minister, is no doubt always being warned by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), and quite properly so, as I was warned before, that we should not undertake responsibilities which are not the constitutional responsibilities of the federal government or of the parliament of Canada.
But this is a problem. The minister no doubt saw the articles that were published recently about Schefferville. The minister is well aware, I know, of the situation at Red Lake. One could go on and give many other similar instances, but this problem is one that-I am not being critical-it is not easy to solve; it is extremely difficult to solve. As a matter of fact, one of the difficulties about solving this is that it is so little understood, and it does seem to me that the committee should concentrate, at any rate for a part of its time, upon methods of solving this particular problem, of really seeking to get in all of those provinces where there are


Indians, or any considerable number of Indians, a clear understanding with the provincial governments of where the federal responsibility ends and where the provincial responsibility begins.
Part of the difficulty-and this is where I think the committee could do a great deal of good-is to eradicate this wholly erroneous opinion that the Indians are the wards of the federal government. They are not, and never were wards of the federal government. The Indians are Canadian citizens, like any other Canadian citizens, and the provincial governments have exactly the same responsibility toward them, when they are off a reserve, as they have toward any other citizen of the provinces; but a great many well-meaning, honest and honourable people are betrayed into taking an entirely wrong position with respect to the Indians because of this entirely erroneous opinion that Indians are wards of the federal government, or wards of the crown, which they are not and never were, in their legal status. It is true they are citizens who suffer under a certain disability, and also who enjoy certain advantages that are not enjoyed by other citizens, but that does not make them any less citizens of Canada.
It does not seem to me that I should go beyond these three broad fields which I feel we and the committee should give priority to; but I do appeal to the minister again to try, within the limits of the freedom that we will all want to have in the committee, to give the kind of focus and direction to its activities, to indicate the direction in which the department feels the time has now come to move and that the government would be prepared, given the right objectives, to move, so that what we do in the committee will bear fruit.

Mr. Speaker, naturally, we in the C.C.F. support wholeheartedly the resolution and any activities which may be entered into by the committee or by the department in so far as those activities are helpful not only for our Indian people but for those of us who are not Indians but appreciate and understand the difficulties of the Indian people proper. I was most interested in listening to the comments of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) with respect to an indication from the minister and the government of the things which the government and the minister may have in mind so far as correction is concerned or the hopes they may have with respect to alterations to the act or to the administration. I am sure that if this is done in the manner suggested it will be of some help to the committee in

staying on a fairly straight track. Otherwise the committee will have a tendency to wander all over the field which it should do so far as consideration is concerned and listening to the representations of interested parties, but when it comes to consolidating those representations and developing them into some form that will permit of a plan or program to be followed in the next few years then we might be well advised to consider the ideas of the minister and the department.
In addition, I think there is one thing which the committee should have provided for it-incidentally, this applies to other committees as well. Because of the complexity of the subject, because of the different developments and attitudes among Indians in different parts of the country this committee might well have provided for it fairly extensive research facilities. If this were done then people in the anthropological field, the economic field or the legal field, so far as the effect of treaties not only with the Indians but with others is concerned, could provide the committee with detailed and exhaustive research material which would assist the committee to evaluate properly the various representations made to it.
Since last session, as the minister indicated, a number of people have been anxiously awaiting the establishment of a similar committee this session as was unanimously recommended and as was indicated by the minister. This extreme interest has not been confined to Indian bands or Indian organizations only but other people have also expressed an interest. With respect to the question of representation of Indians in this house directly or through the exercise of the franchise, following the remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate may I say that the two measures which I understand will be dealt with subsequent to this motion will in my opinion be the most beneficial steps that can be taken in that direction.
With respect to Bill No. C-2 and Bill No. C-3 which are slated to be discussed shortly, if I may refer to them briefly I would hope that after they have been given second reading by the house they might be referred to the committee. From reading the terms of the resolution I understand that the committee will be discussing this field and I think that these bills might properly be referred to the committee.
There is one other matter in this regard which I think should be given consideration by the committee and it undoubtedly has been given some thought by the minister with respect to the presentation of the two bills to which I have referred. Following the passage of these bills, and I am quite
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act sure they will be passed, what is to be the relationship between the 122 Indians-I believe that was the figure-who up to now have signed taxation waiver forms pursuant to the Canada Elections Act and the Indian Act and all the other Indians in Canada who will be granted' the franchise without having had to sign such a waiver? I hope that we will not establish two classes of Indians so far as voting is concerned, one class being the 122 who up to this time have taken advantage of the waiver section and consequently have received the right to vote, and the second class being all other Indians on the reserves who have not taken advantage of it.
As an indication of the interest which has been developing since last session with respect to the establishment of this committee, I understand that some 65 to 70 Indian bands have expressed a desire to appear before the committee and' present material to it as well as some 30 organizations, including Indian organizations such as native brotherhoods, and some five provincial governments. I think that is a good thing because in some of these fields there is a conflict between provincial and federal jurisdiction or a lack of a strict line of demarcation. One interesting thing with respect to the provincial governments and which makes me wonder why all the provinces have not expressed interest in appearing before the committee to present their ideas is that one province, which to my knowledge has absolutely no Indians on reserves but which receives a contribution of $70,000 toward Indian day schools, has expressed a desire to appear. I refer to the province of Newfoundland. This makes me wonder why other provinces which have heavy complements of Indians have not yet taken the opportunity to express a desire to appear before the committee to present their ideas. I hope that such provinces as Quebec, which has a large Indian population, Alberta and the other three Atlantic provinces, all of which have not yet expressed a desire to appear before the committee, will undertake to communicate with the committee and appear before it to give it the benefit of their opinions on this all-important question.
Some people may disagree with me but this committee will be dealing with what I consider to be the most important minority group in Canada. Certainly we cannot be too proud of our treatment of the Indians in the past. I hope that the operations of the committee will afford an opportunity to right some of the wrongdoings and broken promises with respect to our native Indian people and
1900	HOUSE OF
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act will be a reflection, I am sure, of the conscious desire of every member of the house to extend to our Indian people a much fairer deal than they have had in the past. I think the work of the committee will certainly have an effect extending beyond Canada. We can be judged to a degree by other nations on the basis of our attitude toward our own people and I hope that the resulting conclusions, recommendations and action will bring about for Canada a position of more respect internationally than we have had in the past with respect to the treatment of our minority groups.
The variety and complexity of the problems confronting our Canadian Indians are much greater than confront other groups of people in Canada. Certainly the Indians in some fields have the same problems and difficulties as many other people but in addition they have special and peculiar problems. I was very pleased that the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate, and I am sure he had no difficulty in doing so, selected as the most important question that of education. The work of the committee should not be confined to the question of providing the formal type of educational opportunities for Indian children but should be expanded to cover education in the relationships between the Indians and other groups in our society.
Also-and this is probably a question of the public relations feeling of the Indian affairs branch itself-in this question of education there should be some education directed to those of us who are not Indians so that we shall have a better understanding of the Indian himself, his background and history, his problems and his hopes. The committee should not think of this thing in terms of a one-way street only, of imparting to the Indian children and the Indian population those things which we as non-Indians think they should learn. It should be a twoway street. There should be a desire to have a mutual understanding and appreciation of each other's backgrounds, cultures, and aptitudes.
These backgrounds, degrees of education and understanding and economies of the Indians vary from one part of the nation to the other. For instance, there are the Indians comprising the Six Nations group. Their close proximity to the United States and their easy access to the country across the border-the fact that they were resident there long before the border was established in the first place-has allowed the Six Nations people to develop a slightly different attitude and a slightly different understanding of things, of our economy and of the way in


which they should be related to our economy than those of the Indians along the coastal part of British Columbia whose primary way of providing for themselves in years past has been through fishing and through trapping. They developed a different culture and a different understanding and they now have a different attitude. The Indians on the plains or in the prairie provinces accordingly developed in a different way, with different backgrounds, and have reached different stages of education as compared with Indians in other parts of the nation.
Taking into account all of this variety of rates of growth, differences in cultural background, differences in education, the committee will have them reflected in the various briefs or presentations and oral arguments presented before it and that will be good. I think the committee needs to have an understanding of the variety of problems of the different groups and different backgrounds the various Indian peoples have. However, there is an ancient Chinese saying to the effect that one look is worth a thousand reports. I think the committee, in addition to sitting, receiving briefs, asking questions and attempting to understand the presentations and the problems that are dealt with, might profitably undertake-and whether it has this authority, I do not know; if it has not, it should seek it-to arrange for visits by the committee to selected and various sections of the nation in order to see at firsthand particularly the social conditions on the reserves, the housing problem and the economic conditions of the Indians.
These matters can never be appreciated by listening to a brief presented by anybody but they certainly can be practically brought home by visiting some of the reserves and some of the areas, especially those fringe areas to which the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate referred; that is to say areas on the fringe of an industrially developed area. They are not Indians now. They are not on the reserves. They are in some limbo period in between.
If the committee could undertake to select a few areas-for instance in the Northwest Territories-where it will see and be able to appreciate some of the conditions that exist there-it would be helpful. I think probably the coastal part of British Columbia or the interior part of British Columbia reflects a different group, a different attitude, different conditions than do Alberta and the prairie provinces. The committee might visit some selected areas there. I am sure it will have dramatically and graphically drawn to its attention some of the conditions there. I would also mention the Six Nations, the

people in the maritimes and so on. All this would be a tremendous asset to the members of the committee in being able to appreciate more fully some of the social and economic problems confronting the native Indian person on the reserve itself.
I know many native Indian people. We have a large complement of them in northern British Columbia. I know many of them personally and have visited their villages and their homes. I have had correspondence from other Indians I have come to know during the past few years. I know they have extremely high hopes for the result arising out of this committee functioning. It is not only the Indians who have high hopes. But certainly those are the ones whose activities, interest and welfare should be kept in mind throughout the functioning of this particular committee. In its consideration of the problems, its reception of briefs and in its Anal recommendation I hope the committee will not disappoint either the Indians or anyone else in the hopes they have for something beneficial arising out of the efforts of the committee.

I should like to say a word or two in conection with the appointment of this committee since I had the privilege last November of sitting in for two days at the meeting of the general council of the Indians of Alberta and hearing the resolutions which they desire to present to this committee upon its formation. I was rather amazed to find the change of attitude on the part of the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) who was the previous minister of this department. I recall an instance in 1956 when his, in my opinion, little knowledge of his department almost led to the severance from the band in Hobbema of some 117 Indians who had every right to live there. I think the sooner this committee can get formed and get to work, the sooner this committee can hear representations from Indians all across Canada so that their ideas will be incorporated in any changes which may be made to the act. I may say that the council meeting I attended discussed and approved 29 resolutions and they are anxiously waiting to have them presented to this committee. I presume that would be the case with respect to Indian bands and Indian councils all across Canada.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate also paid some attention apparently to trying to direct the affairs of this committee.
I should like to suggest to him that this matter will be in capable hands.
The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) made mention of the fact that five of the
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act provincial governments will send representations and he chastised in a mild way the government of the province of Alberta. But I suggest to him that perhaps the government of Alberta feel that the federal representatives of the constituencies in which there are Indians will take care of the interests of the Indians in those constituencies, as we are elected to represent our Indians as well as non-Indians.

I did not want to interrupt the hon. member while he was speaking, but I believe I have a right to make a correction of something he said in his speech. He said that I had changed my attitude since certain events at Hobbema. I should like to remind the hon. gentleman that as soon as my advice was taken, and that case was taken into the courts where it should have been taken in the first place, justice was done.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to tell the minister that the proposed committee is certainly likely to help achieve the purpose in view, that of meeting various personalities who are to consider the position of the Canadian Indians. But I wonder how this committee will be able to obtain the general views of our Indians. As you know, Indians have a deep distrust of white men, and I don't blame them for feeling this way, because they are perfectly right.
In fact, when we go back into history we see just what white men brought to the Indians, who had been absolute masters of this American continent to which they had a primary right.
The first thing that Cartier did after landing at Gaspe was to kidnap two Indians that he took back to France with him and exhibited to the French as new specimens of what were considered almost as monkeys.
Then, Champlain, just to show the greatness of white men, used his musket to shoot down those poor helpless Indians.
Later on, the English and the French, with their fire-water, attempted to steal pelts from those poor savages who did not know of their value.
Later, again by means of fire-water, the Indians-to whom we have too long referred to as savages, in a deprecatory sense-were led to take part in wars and to be killed on behalf of the white men.
1902	HOUSE OF
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act
We also know that, in western Canada, Indians and half-breeds were dispossessed of their property in favour of the Canadian Pacific.
Mr. Speaker, what have the white men given them in return? Tuberculosis was unknown among those people. White men transmitted that germ to those people who were then decimated for centuries, the government having felt in recent years the necessity of intervening and of dealing with the matter. That disease had been brought to the Indians by white men.
Before the arrival of white men, Indians of Canada respected individual property and did not seek to appropriate it for themselves. They hunted, accumulated a stock of pelts, which they stored in trees and picked up intact in the spring. It was the white man who taught the Indian to steal.
A missionary, not too familiar with Indian customs, had gone visiting several Indian villages. He and his Indian guide came to a lake shore on which they pulled up their canoe containing provisions for several weeks. The Indian took out some of the provisions, leaving the rest in the canoe. The missionary asked how much food was left and the Indian replied: "We have enough to last us until tomorrow."
The priest said: "Is there no danger of this food being stolen?" And the Indian replied: "No, Father, there are no white men around."
So, that evil, and theft, was brought from Europe by white men.
Therefore, I am inclined to believe that we will not be able to gather here all those people who should be here, all the Indians who should be consulted, before anything is imposed on them.
When and how will we be able to know their view?
The committee may produce certain documents, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Smith) said, but what tribes will come here and make their views known?
The bands that sat for two days and prepared twenty nine resolutions will certainly come. But do they represent the majority of Indians? I do not think so.
I know that most of the Indians of the province of Quebec do not seem to be in favour of this bill, not because they do not want to vote, but because they fear the white man; they are afraid that, in exchange for a favour, the white man will take something away from them. They have been given reservations, yes, but the areas of those reservations have been cut down, and besides their sites have been changed when it seemed


necessary to do so to make room for the white man. Because of all these things, the Indians no longer trust the white man- (Text):
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, the hon. member is not discussing the motion before the house. He is discussing amendments which are now before the house in Bill No. C-2 and Bill No. C-3, I think.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I am afraid the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Speakman) is completely wrong. I am just proving that it will be practically impossible to get the point of view in that committee of the Indians, because they do not believe in the white people. I cannot discuss this matter when Bill No. C-2 is presented to the house. Mr. Speaker, if we are to reach the Indians we will have to do so in some other way, such as a referendum, and that is what I am trying to establish. ^ I believe I have the right to do so at this time on the presentation of this motion to form a committee.

That is what I meant, Mr. Speaker. There is only one way to go about it and it would be to attempt, through some kind of organization, to spread useful information among all our Indian bands of the province of Quebec and elsewhere.
We often talk about the bill of rights, but are we doing anything to allow every Indian to speak for himself and in his own right, as he is entitled to, so that we could be told what he wants? This is what I am asking for. I ask that the committee find some way to convene in Ottawa all the Indians in this country. I am very interested in the problems of our Indian population, and I wish to bring to the attention of the house the contributions which the Indian people have made.
The Indians have fought side by side with their fellow Canadians in two wars, and while those who served in the Canadian army have had their right to vote at federal elections, those who were too old or too young for army service did not have voting privileges. Chief Walking Buffalo, an 88-year old retired chieftain of the Stoney Indians of western Canada, speaking at a meeting on Mackinac island, Michigan, last November, stood up and said:
I stand before you with no jealousy, no pride, no bitterness against any race or any nation in the whole world.
As we are now considering the setting up of this committee and, in addition, a bill which will grant the right to vote to the Indian population, I could not let this occasion go by without passing on to hon. members the words of this wise old Indian who has perhaps more reason to be sceptical of the white man's promises than most other people in the world.
I believe that the key to a new future for the Indians of Canada is for our governments -and I mean all levels of government-to extend to them not only the right to vote but the right to all our educational facilities. If we fail to give them what I consider to be their just due, such a failure would amount to a betrayal of good faith.
The minister made a statement last year to the effect that education is the key to a promising future for the Indians. I fully agree with that statement, and I urge the minister to implement her good intentions and to transform those intentions into a policy to make educational facilities available to every Indian child.
Last September, at my invitation, Senator Gladstone paid a visit to the Ojibwa Indian


band at Fort William. We had a meeting in the Chippewa park pavilion, attended by 200 Indians, the mayor and aldermen of the city, and other elected representatives. The senator addressed the gathering and stressed the need for Indians to acquire the same status and rights as any other citizens without endangering their treaty rights. After the speeches he talked to many of the members of the local reserve. The meeting served to point out the fact that the Indian cannot make his living under the old treaty rights of fishing and trapping alone. Their children should be kept in school until they reach the age of 18, and better arrangements should be made with the secondary schools to enable them to attend. Transportation to and from the schools, which are generally several miles away from the children's homes, should be provided.
These are problems affecting the Indian population of the district of Thunder Bay, and I have no doubt they have application to other parts of Canada. Indians in other areas may have different problems, but in the main one is bound to admit that the general status of these original Canadians is much below the standard enjoyed by the rest of the population. Only recently I heard a report to the effect that Indians in Manitoba were on a semistarvation diet. If it is true, this is a serious indictment of our entire Indian policy.
I cannot think of a better way to plead on behalf of the Indian people for a better understanding of their problems than by quoting from one of the many Indian legends in which Indian lore is so rich. Begochiddy, the god of creation, approached twin boys out on a hunt and told them they had been born of the sun and must now visit their father. He gave them a ray of light and a rainbow to help them make the long journey into the heavens. He told them that of all things their father might offer they must bring back only the flint armour, the lightning arrows, the stone knife and a magic fire stick.
The twins rode the light and the rainbow over deep canyons, rivers and sky-piercing mountains. The time passed quickly, daybreak, the afterglow of sunset, the dusk and the darkness, until they reached the house where the spirit of the sun lived with other heavenly spirits and his messenger the dragonfly. To make certain the boys were his own, the sun put them through severe trials. He threw them onto spikes, smothered them with steam, exposed them to storms and freezing nights. The boys convinced their father by enduring all the tortures and then the twins returned by rainbow and light to the earth, carrying the magic weapons.

The Indians, as in legend, have in reality been smothered with the steam of promises, they have been exposed to storms and freezing nights because of poor shelters, and heaven knows they have been exposed to prejudice.
I wish to quote briefly from a study of attitudes toward Indians and people of Indian descent made by a sociologist of the University of Manitoba and by Fraser Earle, regional director of the Canadian council of Christians and Jews who in their conclusions state:
The Indian will live among, and have contact with, people whose general level of education is closer to his own when he comes into the urban centre. The Indian has a general level of education that averages grade six. The white population has a general education which averages about grade nine. The Indian will be more likely to deal with persons of lower educational standing in terms of social contact, than with people whose education is advanced. It is more likely that the Indian will be in contact with people having elementary school education or none at all, rather than in social contact with persons of university education.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Mr. Speaker, I am asking
leave of the house merely to finish my quotation because it is pertinent to what I am discussing in relation to the Indian problem which will be taken up by the committee. I continue the quotation as follows:
Persons who completed elementary school objected vigorously to the suggestion that their children should play with Indian children. There was no objection to this suggestion among university graduates. To the question about including Indians in a party in the home, eighteen point six per cent (18.6 per cent) of the elementary school group objected. None of the university group objected. Similarly, eighteen point two per cent (18.2 per cent) without formal education objected to Indians being hired as teachers; there was a much weaker objection by university educated people. In general, there is a good deal of resistance to Indians being given status in the many situations where it is required. By this we mean, having their children play with Indian children, go to school with Indian children, being taught by an Indian. These suggestions met more resistance from people with little education as compared with those having advanced education.
The conclusion is that there is not a widespread incidence of extreme prejudice toward Indians and persons of Indian descent, but, enough prejudice exists in significant areas of contact that its effect will be felt by the Indians. The persons he is most likely to work with and have social contact with in the urban centre, are the people who seem to be more highly prejudiced toward him.
It appears from our survey that the degree of contact, or the information that people have, about Indians, has little to do with their attitudes toward them. People with no information about or contact with Indians were as prejudiced in as many situations as those persons having contact and having information. This would seem to confirm a statement made in the introduction that stereotypes are accepted uncritically by some people. It may also be concluded that more education makes people more tolerant of the Indian's need to be accepted and recognized in the community.
What we really need is a better understanding of the Indian people by encouraging intermingling and friendly intercourse with the people of other origins.
The suggestion made by the hon. member for Skeena to enable members of the committee to visit some of the reserves where conditions may warrant such a visit is a valuable suggestion. Perhaps the minister would select the reserves to be visited.
I believe that the Indians of our generation have earned the right to better housing and

Joint Committee to Study Indian Act to equal opportunities for education, employment and a general improvement of their standards of living. I submit that this government should without undue delay give our Indians a new charter, a charter of equality enjoyed by all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, as one who was a member of a similar committee last year and as one who comes from one of the areas of Canada with the most concentrated Indian population along the British Columbia coast I wholeheartedly support the setting up of this committee. Unfortuately, there was not time last year for too much progress to be made by the committee, but we did have a sufficient number of meetings to enable us to grasp some understanding of what we might accomplish, and we heard some excellent witnesses.
I am sorry that the Indians across the river do not trust their white neighbours in Hull, because the Indians who came down here to meet the committee seemed to have full confidence in the fact that this government was prepared to give them a fair shake. We had the Reverend Dr. Peter Kelly, who is a native Indian and was born on the Queen Charlotte islands in the Haida tribe and Robert Clifton, one of my near neighbours and president of the native brotherhood of British Columbia. This is an indication of the type of spokesman that we can expect to have before this committee.
I am sorry I have not my copy of Longfellow with me because I might cite Hiawatha, but I think the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) gave us enough literature today.
One thing that has concerned me has been what is to me the appalling waste of manpower that is allowed to go on with regard to our Indian population. Our Indian population is approximately 180,000. I do not know how many of those would be men able to work but it would be a considerable percentage. As a logging operator on the coast of British Columbia at times I have had the opportunity of employing quite a number of Indians, and it has worked out very well. I have been very pleased with the work they have performed and they appear to have been very happy to work for me.
One of the problems in employment there is the lack of co-ordination among industry, employment bureaus, the Indian population and the Indian officials in order to arrive at some plan where knowledge is available to the employment officers and


to the companies as to where Indians are available for work at certain jobs. They have made excellent workmen in some fields, particularly in the field of machine operation and in the field of rafting and boom work. In those fields they have been outstanding. I have already spoken to the minister about hopes that the department could evolve some scheme whereby a greater use might be made of this potential labour force. I know that attention is being given to it right now; I know it is a problem. One of the main problems with regard to the Indian population all across the country is the lack of interest on the part of business and industry in employing Indians, and I think that business and industry are missing a great opportunity in many instances.
I must say I have been very much impressed with the confidence the Indians have expressed in the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) and in the way she is carrying on her responsibilities. There seems to be a new feeling of confidence, one that has not been there for a long time, and also a new confidence in the officials of the Indian affairs branch of the department, an entirely different attitude from that which obtained not so many years ago.
I am sure that this committee will be a worth-while one; I am sure that it is going to have a tremendous amount of work to do and that it will have to listen to, of course, a large number of witnesses to get a comprehensive picture of the overall problem. I know that the Indians in my area are looking forward with great interest to the establishment of this committee, to the final report and to the amendments which will be forthcoming to the act as a result of the report.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to support this particular motion. In the remarks I make I want to emphasize particularly one topic and that has to do with the relationship of forestry to the Indians. When we look at the figures for the number of Indians in Ontario, which are over 40,000, we realize that the majority of that 40,000 lives in the boreal forest area. I think we are entitled to say we are disappointed at the failure of the Indians living in this particular region to play a larger part in an economic sense in the forestry field.
When we look at the report put out, I believe, in the past year by the Indian affairs

branch on the Canadian Indian-a reference paper-we find that it says on page 17:
Agriculture ranks next to trapping, hunting and fishing in importance, particularly in the prairie provinces, southern Ontario and parts of British Columbia.
If trapping and agriculture are the two main economic fields in which the Indian is drawing his income and at the same time the majority of the Indians in Ontario are living in the boreal forest region, which also happens to support Ontario's greatest industry, it seems that the Indians, or the Indian affairs branch, have been missing an opportunity, which I think should be the subject of the committee's study.
The pull of the Indians in my particular constituency, in the west and the north and to the east in the Cochrane area, is more and more in the last decade toward some kind of gainful opportunity and employment on a steady basis and away from the rather nomadic kind of existence they have had. The minister has had a prize illustration of this in the conundrum which she has faced recently over the establishment of an Indian reservation at Macdiarmid, Ontario. Mac-diarmid happens to be on the east side of lake Nipigon and a number of Indians have moved there on their own. I am pleased to note that the branch has taken action and is going to erect a number of houses there and in fact establish a reserve.
I do not want to go into the bitterness that emerged in the community over this particular move. I am on the side of the Indian affairs branch in establishing the reserve there. In my talks with the Indians at this particular place it was interesting to me to realize how keen they are now to get into some kind of basic employment. They realize that that employment must fit into the regular picture of employment in the boreal forest. Of course, the regular picture of the boreal forest, if you want to work at it, has to tie in with mining, with forestry or with transportation. We can rule out the field of technical aspects of mining and of transportation in boreal forests for Indians these days, but we can expect a greater contribution and a greater opportunity for the Indians on the pulp and paper limits and in the pulp and paper operations. This is separate from the forested land which the Indians themselves have, but about which I want to make some remarks in a few minutes.
It seems to me that this particular committee, in so far as it is studying economic and social aspects of the Indian problem, especially in Ontario-and I think this spills over into northern Manitoba, into the boreal section of Saskatchewan, and perhaps of Alberta-there is not anything more important 79951-0-120J
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act than the development of a policy that will give the Indians work on bush operations within the pulp and paper industry where there is a growing stability of operation and growing opportunity.
I have told the house and the minister before that it is not easy to get our Indians from Ontario to do this kind of work on a constructive and consistent basis. They tend to work for a week or two, get a bit of money and away they go. It takes a great deal of encouragement and a great deal of patience on the part of employers, contractors or anyone having anything to do with Indians. They do not come naturally to a settled working existence in the woods side of the pulp and paper industry but if we do not make the effort it seems to me that the only thing left for the Indian in our particular kind of country is as a sort of picturesque guide without too much basic means of earning a living because you cannot mistake the fact that northern Ontario, all the way from Kenora eastward to Sudbury and to the north, is becoming more and more a summer dormitory for the American midwestern states. The movement in of United States tourists and also the development of a patchwork of roads and consolidation of operations by the large pulp and paper companies means that the old traditional existence based upon trapping, fishing and drawing subsistence from the land itself just is not possible any more and is becoming more and more difficult for the Indian.
This is the explanation of why 120 Indians have drifted away from the east shore of lake Nipigon, where they had, I think, a rather good establishment, where they were well supported by the Indian affairs branch, to the magnet of the highway and opportunities for gainful employment of some continuing kind.
It seems to me that with this kind of development taking place in this country, with the movement in of the tourists, with the consolidation and stabilization of the pulp and paper operations, we have to make a strenuous, planned effort that will require much patience and a certain minimum amount of technical education in order to enable our Indians to draw an income from the kind of existence that is based upon jobs as pulp cutters, bush workers, timber cruisers and so on. At the presnt time very few Indians in our area are successful.
One of the places I should like the committee to visit is Pickle Crow which happens to be in my constituency. I worked there as; a miner before the war and I can still remember the shock I felt the first day I was in Pickle Crow. I came out of the cookhouse
1908	HOUSE OF
Joint Committee to Study Indian Act and there were a number of garbage cans there. I could see these figures scrabbling around the garbage cans with flies in clouds all around. I asked who they were and someone remarked, "Those are our blueberry blondes". It was a bunch of squaws digging in the garbage pails.
Pickle Crow Gold Mines made an effort during the war because of the manpower shortage to see if they could not utilize some of the Indians in various operations around the mines. From letters I have had from several acquaintances who work there it appears that Pickle Crow have had rather phenomenal success in the light of the general tendency of the bush Indian to shy away from a regular kind of routine. From the information I have I gather there is enough of an example at Pickle Crow in the use of Indians, particularly on surface work and in cutting timber and that kind of thing fitting into the underground operations, to make it a place well worth visiting by the committee or a subcommittee. They could see whether the plan that has worked at Pickle Crow could not be extended on a much wider basis and also whether the kind of approach which was used there could not be effective with the pulp and paper companies.
If this were done I think the committee might come up with practical recommendations which would enable us to get the Indian into something that will give him the kind of pride and confidence that I have noticed among certain Indians at Macdiarmid who through their own organizing ability have managed to get fishing contracts and pulp-wood cutting contracts and as a result have gone away up in the scale. One man there who is the leading Indian in the community said to me, "I haven't any education but by God I am going to get it for my children whether the Indian affairs branch will do it or not". He did not have any particular chip against the Indian affairs branch but he felt that this just had to come.
When I see an example like that I can overlook all the drunken Indians you may see on the streets of Kenora, Hornepayne, Nakina and other northern towns where they tend to be a bit of a joke, where they are sort of looked upon as riff-raff and are tossed out of the beer parlours all the time late on Saturday night. Some of you may think that is loose talk. It is not. I was born in northwestern Ontario. I spent most of my time in the bush and in the bush communities, and the Indian has never had much status there. It is a real tragedy.
A few years ago I taught a boy who went as far as any Indian from northwestern Ontario ever did, at least up to that time. He


got to first year university and then he finally failed. I spent quite a bit of time tutoring him and I knew his capabilities. He had average capabilities and with a great deal of work he could have made it through university. Somehow he was not able to apply himself and I think it was because of his home conditions. I know what they were and they were not good. I saw him two years later and I was terribly disappointed because he had reverted right back. You would never know this was the alert, bright boy who had been reading Trevelyan and other such works. He was right back almost in the worst of conditions in so far as clothes and everything else was concerned.
So you have to follow through all the way with the Indians in our part of the country and be prepared for tremendous disappointments. That is why I hope the committee will not be one of those dundering committees that ambles and meanders along. I hope that all members of the committee will realize the seriousness of the problem and the tremendous achievements they can make in terms of recommending and developing policy.
I want to make some remarks about forest policy so far as Indian lands in Canada are concerned. The minister's office was good enough to make a return in answer to a question I placed on the order paper. We have in Canada at the present time approximately 2,400 square miles of Indian reserve lands that the department believes are capable of intensive forest management. In her return the minister answered my question as to how many professional foresters are at the disposal of the department in order to implement forest management plans.
I know that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. McQuillan), for example, could argue that the number of professional foresters is not necessarily a valid indicator of how well you are approaching the management of forested land, but when you consider that there are very few people in the Indian affairs branch who have forestry experience on the forest management side, when you consider that there are no Indians in eastern Canada anywhere to my knowledge who have professional experience in forestry, these figures are rather sad. I asked a question as to how much of this land was now under forest management and got these figures. In British Columbia there are 900 square miles that could be under forest management but only 400 square miles are. In Alberta there are 100 square miles that could be under forest management and none is. As to Saskatchewan, they do not know

how much land there could be under forest management and so the answer is none. In Manitoba the same situation exists.
In other words, in the two eastern prairie provinces, despite the number of Indians they have in the boreal forest area, there is no conception of how much land could be put under forest management; in fact, no conception of the forest management aspect at all. So far as Ontario is concerned, there are 1,250 square miles that could be under the forest management and approximately 1,000 square miles are.

should like to have a little bit to say on this motion, Mr. Speaker. We are all exceedingly pleased that the committee on Indian affairs is going to be reconvened. I am particularly happy about it, having had a great interest in the Indians in British Columbia for the past 25 years. I want to express the hope that it is going to be a working committee that will face up to the issues and to the realities of the situation with regard to the economy and the social conditions of our native Indian population


today, with the idea of bringing about recommendations for policies that will, in their eventuality, mean a real integration of a native Indian population with all others.

I think it is high time that we really gave thought to them. In speaking about the appointment of a committee and about the first and the real Canadians it is quite easy to express a sloppy sentimentality and emotionalism and perhaps even some suggestions of money spent and jobs done. But the fact remains that we have not done a good job for them.
The resolution which is now before us is one asking not only for the authority to appoint a joint committee, but in the opening paragraph sets out the terms of reference. I am most interested in the part which says-
-authority to investigate and report upon Indian administration in general and, in particular, on the social and economic status of the Indians:
As was pointed out by the previous speaker, much as I think all hon. members would like to be on that committee, such of course is not possible. Therefore it is only when this motion is before the house that, under those terms of reference I have referred to, we have an opportunity of giving an indication of what we trust is meant by the minister in using the words "the social and economic status of the Indians". If such a study is going to be done on a factual and realistic basis, a lot of hard realities will have to be faced by the members of that committee, and I sincerely hope and trust that such matters are faced. Subjects which I hope are included in the words "social and economic status" are matters appertaining to education, to community services, to welfare, to employment, to the maintenance of Indian culture and to the development of Indian crafts.
I hope that the interpretation of those words in the terms of reference will allow in particular a study of the question of education of Indians, because, Mr. Speaker, although I know it is a matter of a controversial nature I have felt for a long time that something is wrong with government policy where, from the cradle and right through the years of childhood education, the education of Indians in the main is on a segregationist basis. They are educated on a separate schools basis for native Indians only, and when they come from those schools and enter the Canadian economy they are expected to become assimilated and able to carry on.

Over the years British Columbia has made some advances in integrating the native children in the schools, and I think it has worked out exceedingly well. I hope that that is one of the phases which will be studied. The committee should investigate whether or not you can look after the social and economic needs of Indians if they are kept completely segregated in their childhood and their educational period in life.
I hope, that the terms of reference mean that a real study is going to be made of the community services and the social welfare of our native Indians. It is unfortunate, I think, that when they approach their teens and their adulthood and try to come into the general economy they are ignored and neglected. I think one reason for this is that we expect our Indian agents to be social welfare workers, which they are not although they have to spend a great deal of time being so.
In addition to all those aspects-and I do not want to take up too much time-is the question of employment. I feel that we have a responsibility in this committee when dealing with the economic status and welfare of Indians not to expect them to have to go outside the reservations completely because there is no employment in their immediate area. With the funds at the disposal of the department, or if they have not got the funds, through the medium of government, there should be a policy of developing the Indians in their economy if we are not going to make provision for them to be assimilated into the general economy outside of their own native economy.
So I say, Mr. Speaker, that to me this is a most important committee. We have had them in the past and they have done a fairly good job, although a great deal has fallen through. Personally, I feel as a member of parliament, and previous to that as a member of the legislature, that we have betrayed the native Indians of our country, because by this time they should have been assimilated as first class citizens. I feel a great deal of the responsibility for that is not on the native Indians but on ourselves, and I sincerely hope that the terms of reference, in particular the reference to the social and economic status of the Indians and the administration of the department and matters of legislation, mean what they say and that we are going to have a committee which really studies these questions, controversial as they may be, and then bring in recommendations of a wonderful nature and present them to a government with the fortitude to follow through.

Mr. Speaker, during the recess last year it was my privilege to travel some 10,000 miles and visit 53 bands representative of over 220 reserves. In the course of those travels, which I made by way of plane, train, automobile and boat, I saw many and different situations. You cannot have a common rule, as was said, I think, by the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), which would be applicable to all of the Indians in Canada. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-2, to amend the Indian Act.
She said: The purpose of this bill is, in conjunction with Bill No. C-3, to remove the restrictions which presently stand in the way of the Indians of Canada exercising the federal franchise on an equal basis with other citizens.
It will come as a surprise to most members to learn that as far back as 1885 many of the Indians in Canada had the right to vote in federal elections. Prior to that date, the qualifications for voting in federal elections were governed by provincial acts but the franchise act of 1885 gave the right to vote to Indians living in all provinces east of Manitoba. The records reveal that Indians in Ontario, Quebec, and the maritime provinces exercised their franchise in the general elections of 1887, 1891 and 1896, in some instances at polling subdivisions established on reserves.
In 1898 the franchise act was repealed thus providing that provincial voters lists would again govern in determining the entitlement of persons eligible to vote in federal elections. As a result, the majority of the Indians lost their right to vote for ordinarily they were not on the provincial voters lists and in most cases were specifically disqualified as electors. Although Indian veterans of world wars I and II were granted the franchise in 1920 and 1944 respectively, and although their wives were given the franchise in 1948, the situation remained unchanged for the majority of the Indians until 1950, as they were disquali-

fled as electors by the 1920 dominion elections act.
During the late 1940's a special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons investigated Indian affairs and in its report recommended that the federal franchise be granted to all Indians. Amendments to the Canada Elections Act in 1950 and the Indian Act in 1951 implemented this recommendation in part. Indian veterans and their wives, and Indians ordinarily resident off reserves were given the franchise on the same basis as other citizens. However, the bulk of the Indian population, those ordinarily resident on reserves, were required to waive their statutory right to exemption from taxation on or in respect of personal property held on their reserves before they could exercise the franchise.
The proposal now before the house is that the restriction which applies to the Indians living on reserves be abolished so that all Indians will have the right to vote on the same basis as other citizens. Many reasons can be forwarded in support of this proposal. Foremost is the fact that it is not in keeping with our democratic principles that there should be citizens- and all Indians are citizens-who are restricted in the exercise of one of the fundamental rights of a democracy, the right to participate in the election of their repre-sentives in parliament.
Second, however well-intentioned, the present legislation has fallen far short of the objective recommended by the special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons.
Third, the present legislation has been quite unacceptable to the majority of the Indians resident on reserves, as is evidenced by the fact which I mentioned previously this afternoon, that since 1950 only 122 Indians out of an estimated 60,000 adult Indians residing on reserves have waived their exemption to taxation.
Fourth, in recent years more and more Indians and Indian groups have been pressing for the franchise free from the existing restriction.
Finally, there is the reason mentioned by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in his speech to this house on January 18, namely that it will remove in the eyes of the world any suggestion that in Canada

colour or race places any citizen in an inferior category to other citizens of the country.
My comment that many Indians and Indian organizations have been pressing for the vote free from the existing restrictions was not intended to create the impression that all Indians are in favour of having the vote. There are some who are opposed, and their objection is apparently based on the fear that it will mean the loss of aboriginal or treaty rights. I am not aware of any legal basis for this fear and I would like to repeat again the assurance given to the Indians by the Prime Minister in this house on January 18, that existing rights and treaties, traditionally or otherwise, possessed by the Indians, will not in any way be abrogated or diminished in consequence of their having the right to vote.
The Prime Minister has stated that the granting of the federal franchise to Indians is long overdue. I hope that all members will agree that such is the case and that the passing of this bill will mark a new milestone in the advancement of the Indian people towards a fuller participation in the affairs of our country.
