Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset, not merely for myself but on behalf of the party to which I belong in this house, that we intend to support the principle of this bill without any reservation whatsoever. I know that in saying that I am taking a position different from the position which was taken by Mr. Harris in 1951 and 1952 when this subject was last before parliament.
I have taken the trouble to read Mr. Harris' excellent presentation and I do not think there is any question that the arguments he put forward at that time are just as valid today as they were then. I have also looked at what was said by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) in 1952 when the Indian Act was completely revised and I agree with what he said at that time to the effect that the arguments used by Mr. Harris would be of unquestioned validity if applied to any but the aboriginal inhabitants of this country.
The fact is that whatever the legal basis of the tax exemption may be-and I do not intend to enter into a discussion of that today because I think I could be ruled out of order for doing so and in any case I do not think it 79951-0-121
Indian Act
matters; it certainly does not matter to the argument I am putting forward now-whether it is merely statutory or whether it is, as Mr. Drew suggested it was in the debates at that time, something inherent in the status of Indians, it is nevertheless something that most of the Indian people feel is a right.
I am sure that is the reason why despite the hopes that were held in 1952-53, most of the Indians did not execute this waiver; because, in fact, of course this exemption from taxation of income earned on the reserves does not amount to very much; it is not very much that the treasury is losing and it is not very much in the most of cases the Indians would be giving up, but it is a right they believe they have. I am quite sure the hon. lady is quite right when she says the evidence is that the present law is not going to result in many of the Indians exercising the franchise as is clearly indicated by the statistics she gave today that only 122 of them have executed this waiver. Therefore I say that as far as we are concerned we intend to support the principle of this bill.
In a moment I am going to suggest to the hon. lady that I think there are one or two things that could be done that would make this measure much more acceptable, or perhaps I should say much less objectionable, to those Indians, that rather considerable minority of Indians who are either actively opposed to it or very suspicious of it. The hon. lady herself has pointed out that there are many of these Indians.
There are some Indians, of course, who deny that they are Canadian citizens, as I said earlier this afternoon, and who would themselves on no account exercise the franchise, but I do think that for the majority of Indians, including a good number I have talked to, they are not really genuinely anxious to deny the vote to other Indians as long as there is no obligation placed on them to exercise the vote themselves and, as long as at the same time they are quite sure that this is not the thin edge of the wedge which is being inserted by parliament between them and their traditional treaty or other rights.
It seems to me there are certain improvements that the minister could introduce. I am rather glad she will have the opportunity overnight to consider this with the officials because I think there are certain things we could all agree to do. I am simply going to

Indian Act
put them forward as suggestions at this stage. I feel that these suggestions, if implemented, would make this legislation more acceptable or less objectionable.
The first thing I think we ought to do is get an opinion from the minister as to whether the effect of the legislation now before us will be to cancel the existing waivers. If the hon. lady has a legal opinion that it does cancel the waivers for sure, all well and good, but it has been suggested to me-and I do not pretend to know enough about the law to be positive in this case-that if one looks at the Interpretation Act, all this bill will do is to allow all Indians to vote whether or not they have signed the waiver but that the 122 Indians who have signed the waiver will be left under a permanent disability as opposed to other Indians.
As I say, I hope at some stage the hon. lady will give us an opinion from the deputy minister of justice, the law officer of the crown, on that point. I think we should be reassured not just by the hon. lady's assurances but by a legal opinion on this point or, to make absolutely sure, we should put an express provision in the bill to cancel the waivers. That is the first point.
The second point is that either in this bill or possibly preferably in the other bill-I hope Your Honour in view of the interlocked character of them will not be too strait with me over an allusion to it

but in one or the other we should, either by way of preamble or by way of express provision, state that the conferring of the vote upon the Indians does not affect any other of their rights. I am not proposing any language. I am sure that the hon. lady with the advice she could get from the lawyers could find a wording much better than any I could suggest.
I quite agree with the hon. lady that we have no intention of taking away any of their rights but if it were put in the legislation itself, in one of the bills or acts and maybe even in both, it would be desirable. We should do anything we can to give an additional assurance to the Indians that we are not engaged in any scurvy tricks. I am not seeking to put this forward in a partisan spirit. I believe we all want to accomplish the same thing here and we all want to give the maximum assurance.
What I say next is relevant to the bill in a broad sense but not in a narrow sense. This is an act to amend the Indian Act.

The minister and I would not disagree about section 112 of the present act, I am sure. When I was minister I said I would never use that section. I also pledged that the first time I ever brought amendments to the act before the house I would move for its repeal. I do not think there would be any quarrel in the house if we included an amendment in this bill repealing section 112 of the act. That would greatly reassure the Indians because section 112 which is the section relating to compulsory enfranchisement is totally unworkable and I am sure the minister would agree with me about that. The sooner we get it out of the act the better. I do not think it would delay the passage of this measure five minutes and as a matter of fact it might easily expedite it. It would certainly provide a very great deal of reassurance to the Indians.
Apart from that, there is nothing I would say beyond this. I completely agree with the view-and I was never at all happy about it from the time I became the minister of citizenship and immigration-that the Indians should have the vote. I think that much of the misunderstanding of the whole Indian problem in Canada is occasioned by the fact that they do not have the vote, that the whole notion that they have in some way a status different from the status of other citizens arises in the popular mind from the fact that they do not have the vote.
I believe, too, that it is quite wrong that they should not have the vote. I am sure the minister would agree with this view, too. My experience when I was the minister was that in those provinces where the Indians have the vote in provincial elections there is a great deal more attention paid by the provincial governments to the real wishes of the Indians than in those provinces where they do not have the vote.
Were it not against the rules to do so I would express some surprise that in one of the western provinces which prides itself on being exceptionally progressive the vote has never been extended to the Indians. There is no doubt whatever that the moment anyone has a vote in the minds of a great many people aspiring to office, aspiring to election, he does seem to take on a somewhat greater importance. I know that we in this house are all so high minded it would not affect any of us but there are some who have been defeated candidates who, I think, might have been affected by such considerations.
The fact is that the vote is the most priceless of all the possessions of a citizen. To

my way of thinking it is certainly not too soon to be seeing to it that the original citizens of this country have the franchise.

speechtext:
I quite realize that the whole subject of the policy governing the administration of Indian affairs will be coming before the joint committee of this house and the other place which will be set up as soon as the resolution passes this afternoon. While there are special features that are applicable to the Indians of the Yukon territory, yet their problems are much the same as those of people elsewhere in Canada. But in discussing the principle involved in this bill, namely whether or not it is a good thing or a bad thing to provide the right to vote to the Indian people, I want immediately to say that I support the principle of the bill, that is to say that Indian people in Canada should have the right to vote, but I want to consider it in the light of the approach which has been made to the administration of the Indian

Indian Act
Act in the past and relate that administration to the rights which will be acquired by the Indian people if this bill is passed.
We are considering here a bill which in effect will provide the Indian people with the right to vote. This right to vote, in my view, must be distinguished carefully from the obligation to vote, and this apparently is the fear of a good many Indian people in Canada; as it has been described by a substantial minority. Some of the Indian people seem to fear that by the amendment that is now before the house some of their treaty rights will either be abrogated or diminished.
At this point I should like to emphasize my own view, a view which is shared by a good many of the Indian people of the Yukon, a view which they express in the casting of their ballot during a federal election, that progress in the administration of Indian affairs in the country cannot be placed merely on the doing of things for the Indian people. There has been a long experience of the unfortunate results flowing from this indiscriminate paternalism, however well in-tentioned it may have been. Inevitably, inexorably and irrevocably such a program destroys the self-reliance and the initiative of the person it is intended to help by ignoring the basic human right of each individual to decide for himself where his best interests lie. This applies equally and strongly to the bill before the house in as much as this statement of mine can be related to the assertion that it is up to the Indian people themselves to decide for themselves just where their best interests lie in so far as the administration of Indian affairs in the country is concerned, by the.casting of their ballots.
In my submission, our policy should be to minimize the effect of any interference, however benevolent it may be, with the private lives and rights of the Indian people. By this amendment to the Indian Act the Indian people of Canada may, if they wish, but not otherwise, take full advantage of expressing their own desires, their own approval or rejection of federal policies in the field of Indian affairs. They may criticize by their vote the educational policies, the welfare policy, indeed any policy of the branch which affects themselves.
I consider it very important indeed that in working toward the advancement of various Indian groups in the country we must start first with education in the broadest possible sense, just discussed by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). I say "in the broadest possible sense," that is by developing and fostering among the Indian people a deep desire for a better way of life, at any rate what we consider to be a better way of

life; at all times remembering that the individual Indian has every right to regard his existing way of life, if he so chooses to regard it, as the ultimate in a standard of living.
This is sometimes hard for us to understand. On this point I am afraid I am in disagreement with the hon. member for Bon-avista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) because it is not up to us to impose our own views and our own standards upon the Indian people. Integration does not mean assimilation as I believe was mentioned by a member in the far corner a moment ago.
When the Indian himself has taken the first step essential assistance can then be provided to the extent that the Indian people are unable to help themselves. Here I think it is most important to observe that the pace of this development, of these influences which are brought to bear by our policies, is vital. We cannot afford in our impatience to improve conditions among the Indian people to elbow them aside, to displace their own desires and supplant our own views in preference to theirs. It must be left to the Indian people to do those things which they can and which they should and must do for themselves. By providing an opportunity for the Indian people to vote and to have an opportunity to express their own feelings in these matters we will be steering away somewhat from the past propensity to do very undesirable things in the administration of Indian affairs in Canada.
At the same time, if one agrees that what I say is true then the federal authorities must never use this idea that the Indians should be allowed to help themselves and do as they wish as an excuse for failure to provide the basic help that the Indian people need and which they sincerely want and themselves have requested. The decisions as to whether or not to help, how much to give and how far to go are basic to a successful and enlightened administration, and these I believe constitute the most difficult judgments expected of Indian affairs administrators. I realize that all such administrators are human and that mistakes will be inevitable. Nevertheless, these should be and must be kept to an absolute minimum. For this purpose I believe that the administration of Indian affairs in this country must depend heavily upon the help and support of citizen committees such as the one which exists in the Yukon, the Indian advancement association whose activities, under the presidency of Mr. Ted Anderson, are doing much to advance the progress of the Indian people of the Yukon. Such associations, incidentally, are one media whereby the Indian people may express their

opinions and views and acquire facts which will enable them to make their decisions should they choose to exercise their right to vote.
On motion of Mr. Nielsen the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I ask what the business of the house will be for tomorrow and Friday?
Business of the House
Can the house leader also indicate what we will be doing on Monday as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. We should like to continue tomorrow with these two bills dealing with Indian affairs and then, on their completion, to carry on with the resolution in the name of the Minister of Public Works on the subject of national housing; then the resolution in the name of the Minister of Transport dealing with amendments to the Railway Act; and the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister which I have mentioned frequently previously dealing with the tenure of judges. If we can complete those items this week I think we shall begin to show signs of progress in our legislative program. Monday would be private members' day.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: One thing is not quite clear. The house leader indicated that in any event on Friday we would go on with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. I take it now that that is not the intention, and we will carry on with the program as indicated by the house leader?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
My hon. friend has been very co-operative throughout the session, but I did not say "in any event". That question was asked me the other day, and I was quite careful to say that this program was subject to change. I tried to outline the business of the house for several days, but it is hard to estimate the amount of time which will be taken on any one item.
This is what we would like now to do on Thursday and Friday, and complete this portion of the legislative program, which is rather extensive. There are 22 items on the order paper now, and this is the fortieth day of the session. We have the legislative program, all the estimates of the twenty-odd departments, plus the budget debate, which is a fixed debate according to time. If our target date is July 1 then we have to start making rather good progress on some of these items.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Then we will not have agriculture on Friday, I take it?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Not unless we proceed with expedition on the items I have already outlined.
It being fifteen minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
